title: For one another
hookLine: nature made us for one another, so wronging others wrongs the whole (Meditations 9.1)
tomorrow: Death as a work of nature

cards: A cashier gives you too much change. Ten dollars, maybe. Nobody saw.
The store is big; it'll never notice. There may be a small tug anyway, even if it's hard to say why. Book nine of the Meditations opens with Marcus's answer, and it's bigger than ten dollars.
A wrong like that, he says, isn't only against the cashier. It's against the whole.

teach.b: Marcus opens book nine with a startling sentence: whoever acts unjustly acts impiously. A wrong done to a person is also a wrong against the order of things itself.

teach.h: MADE TO HELP, NEVER TO HARM.
teach.b: His reason: nature made rational beings for one another, to help each other as each deserves, and never to harm. So harming someone isn't just breaking a rule.
It's working against what you were made for, and against the nature of the whole, which Marcus here calls the most ancient of divinities. He doesn't stop at cheating.

teach.h: LYING, TOO, IS AT ODDS WITH THE WHOLE.
teach.b: Lying is impiety too, because the nature of the whole is truth, and the liar sets himself at odds with it, whether on purpose or carelessly.

Even being thrown around by pleasure and pain ends up unjust, he says, because it makes us unfair in how we treat people and things. Marcus's view rests on nature and the gods, and not everyone shares it.
But his picture is easy to test on an ordinary day.
The extra ten dollars, the excuse that wasn't true, the credit taken for someone else's work: on his view, none of them stays in its box, because the box was never separate.
For Marcus we're one fabric, and a pulled thread puckers the whole cloth.

how: Readers who take this passage to heart often treat small wrongs as worth fixing even when no one would notice: returning the extra change, correcting the excuse, giving the credit back.

o: one small wrong that puckers the whole cloth
a small mistake that only touches you
a loose end best cut off and forgotten

games.q: for one another — tap the pairs.
p: at odds with a nature that is truth
made to help, never to harm

s: Marcus says a wrong only harms the person it's done to
he calls it impiety too, a wrong against the whole, because nature made us for one another.
in the same entry he calls lying a kind of impiety
the nature of the whole is truth, he says, so the liar is at odds with it.

games.q: the cashier gives you ten dollars too much. nobody saw. you're Marcus with book nine open. what do you do?
o: keep it; the store won't notice.
hand it back: the wrong would be against the whole, not just the store.
keep it, but give the same amount away later.
games.why: Marcus says injustice is impiety: we're made for one another, so even a small wrong works against the whole.

practice: Look back over the last few days for one small wrong you did: a sharp word, a corner cut, a promise that slid, change you didn't hand back. Don't punish yourself; just find it.
Then picture the smallest way to set it right, a message, an apology, a returned thing, a task redone, and see the thread pulling straight.

wordCard.voice: Pulled thread. Marcus's image for one wrong done: it puckers the whole cloth we're woven into. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: injustice, wrongdoing. book nine opens by calling it impiety.

carryVoice: Your line: we're one fabric. On Marcus's view, no wrong stays in its box. That's day six hundred six.
